audience.programmeDescription: Study how people use language, images and media to make meaning and influence others. The regular Groningen pathway is taught in English. A Dutch track is also available.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Groningen combines communication analysis, practical applications and research. The UCR options emphasize discourse and media, workplace and health communication, or digital media and AI.

cellNotes.text: Both study how arguments and persuasive choices shape a message. UCR focuses on rhetoric, public speaking and written argument.
Both examine how language works in interaction. UCR studies turn-taking and dialogue within a broader course on stylistics.
Both address cognitive aspects of language. UCR studies reading and comprehension alongside spoken language and language disorders.
Both study how the material form of a medium shapes communication. UCR traces the technologies and artifacts of media history.
Groningen studies social-media discourse and platform features. UCR examines storytelling and representation across older and newer media.
Groningen studies communication and societal change. UCR courses explore specific examples such as climate communication and racial representation.
Both examine communication in organizations. UCR focuses on leadership, storytelling and persuasion.
Both examine communication in health care. UCR studies consultation and shared decisions within a wider health psychology course.
Groningen has a dedicated intercultural communication course. UCR studies culture and identity across sociology, rhetoric and leadership.
Groningen studies language in context. UCR approaches context through stylistics and social theory.
Both develop academic skills. UCR includes source evaluation, research questions and academic writing.
Both use qualitative research to investigate social meaning. UCR covers interviews, observation and interpretation across a range of social questions.
Both develop statistical analysis. UCR combines statistics with experimental methods and examples from psychology.
Groningen applies quantitative methods specifically to communication. UCR applies these methods in psychology and market research.
Groningen has a dedicated design and evaluation course for communication. UCR offers broader study in research design and measurement.
Groningen’s faculty elective links AI with digital society. UCR explores AI ethics and technical AI methods in separate courses.
Groningen continues its faculty-wide AI theme through a project course. UCR offers separate work in AI ethics, media and data.
Groningen reserves 30 EC for an approved minor.
Groningen studies literacy as a social practice in a dedicated course.
Groningen requires a 10 EC thesis and research seminar. UCR’s optional research element sits outside its degree schedule.
Groningen has a dedicated 10 EC communication case study.

notes.text: The UCR options share methods and topics with Groningen. Groningen combines dedicated courses in language and interaction, communication research, design and evaluation, and a required communication thesis.
This curriculum applies to students starting at Groningen in September 2026.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

source.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

BENENTR211.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
BENENTR211.text: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

BENENTR212.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
BENENTR212.text: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

BENENTR311.name: Market Research
BENENTR311.text: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

source.reviewNote: Compared the retained modal with the revised official description. The revision adds promotional wording without changing the substantive account of planning, conducting and analysing market research; the existing concise text remains faithful.

BENENTR312.name: International Business & Governance
BENENTR312.text: Examines how trade, globalisation and political, cultural and technological conditions shape international business decisions. Students analyse governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate a business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices.

source.reviewNote: Read actual selected current profile; remove confidence/comprehensive-mastery promises and represent concrete methods, projects and limitations proportionately.

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.text: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.

source.reviewNote: CP076: full selected description read against current course evidence; accurate bounded official overview. Retain unchanged text, without adding unstated methods or qualifications.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

BENLEAD111.name: Personal Leadership
BENLEAD111.text: Introduces self-leadership, leadership theory and emotional intelligence. Students use personality and emotional-intelligence profiles to reflect on group dynamics, study leadership cases, and develop a personal plan with practical goals. Assessment tools support educational reflection, with attention to differences in their scientific support.

source.reviewNote: Read actual selected current profile; remove confidence/comprehensive-mastery promises and represent concrete methods, projects and limitations proportionately.

BENLEAD112.name: Leadership Communication
BENLEAD112.text: Studies leadership communication through theory, persuasion, emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Students analyse literary characters, film and speeches, interview a leader, prepare a communication advisory report, and develop an address explaining their own ethical leadership vision.

source.reviewNote: Read actual selected current profile; remove confidence/comprehensive-mastery promises and represent concrete methods, projects and limitations proportionately.

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.text: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

source.reviewNote: Reviewed against the Spring 2027 profile and official description. Omits conditional company collaboration and optional factor analysis; no evidence-source commentary appears in the display text.

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.text: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

BENLEAD312.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
BENLEAD312.text: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.text: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.text: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.text: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.text: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.text: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

GOSHIST312.text: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSSOCI111.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

GOSSOCI214.text: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.text: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.text: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.text: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.text: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

HCBPSYC311.name: Medical & Health Psychology
HCBPSYC311.text: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.

HCBPSYC313.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
HCBPSYC313.text: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.text: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.text: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.text: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.text: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.text: Creative Communication Laboratory combines close reading and creative workshops with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop traditional or hybrid creative projects grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require them to explain their formal, conceptual and procedural choices.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.text: Film & Text studies relationships between literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality. Students learn methods of film analysis and examine plot, character, setting, image, acting, music and sound, alongside the relationships among adaptors, critics and viewers.

MCCLITR312.text: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.text: Introduction to Film & Media examines how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.

MCCMEDI112.text: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.text: From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Television, film and digital forms connect storytelling and power with identity and imagined futures. Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.

Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.text: Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
